body.en: HL Functions deepens the study of mappings and polynomial theory: piecewise modulus transformations, oblique asymptotes of rational curves, Vieta's symmetric polynomial formulas, and complete factorization over the complex field.

label.en: ● Level 1 Foundation — Modulus Function Transformations & Inverses

body.en:
The Modulus (Absolute Value) Function: Defined piecewise by: \[ |x| = \begin{cases} x & x \ge 0 \\ -x & x < 0 \end{cases} \] Cartesian Graph Transformations:

  • \(y = |f(x)|\): Reflects any portion of the curve where \(f(x) < 0\) across the \(x\)-axis into the upper half-plane. Output is strictly non-negative (\(y \ge 0\)). Vertices/cusps occur where \(f(x) = 0\).
  • \(y = f(|x|)\): Erases the left half of the graph (\(x < 0\)) and reflects the right half (\(x \ge 0\)) across the \(y\)-axis. The resulting curve has even symmetry: \(f(|{-x}|) = f(|x|)\).

Injectivity & Inverse Functions: An inverse function \(f^{-1}(x)\) exists if and only if \(f\) is a bijection (one-to-one and onto). For non-injective functions (e.g. parabolas), the domain must be restricted (e.g. \(x \ge h\) where \(h\) is the vertex). The graph of \(y = f^{-1}(x)\) is the reflection of \(y = f(x)\) in the line \(y = x\).

Self-Inverse Property: A function is self-inverse if \(f(f(x)) = x\), or \(f^{-1}(x) = f(x)\). For linear rational functions: \[ f(x) = \frac{ax + b}{cx - a} \implies f(f(x)) = x \quad (\text{symmetric about } y = x). \]

label.en: ▲ Level 2 Analytical Tools — Polynomial Division, Vieta's Relations & Modulus

body.en:
Polynomial Division Algorithm: For any polynomials \(P(x)\) and \(D(x) \neq 0\), there exist unique polynomials \(Q(x)\) and \(R(x)\) such that: \[ P(x) = D(x)Q(x) + R(x), \quad \text{where } \deg(R) < \deg(D). \] Remainder & Factor Theorems:

  • Remainder Theorem: The remainder upon dividing \(P(x)\) by \((x - c)\) is exactly \(P(c)\). If dividing by \((ax - b)\), the remainder is \(P(b/a)\).
  • Factor Theorem: \((x - c)\) is a factor of \(P(x) \iff P(c) = 0\).

Vieta's Formulas (Roots and Coefficients): Let \(P(x) = a_n x^n + a_{n-1}x^{n-1} + \dots + a_1 x + a_0 = 0\) have roots \(\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \dots, \alpha_n \in \mathbb{C}\). Then the elementary symmetric polynomials of the roots satisfy: \[ \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i = -\frac{a_{n-1}}{a_n}, \quad \sum_{1 \le i < j \le n} \alpha_i \alpha_j = \frac{a_{n-2}}{a_n}, \quad \dots, \quad \prod_{i=1}^n \alpha_i = (-1)^n \frac{a_0}{a_n}. \] For a cubic \(ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d = 0\) with roots \(\alpha, \beta, \gamma\): \[ \alpha + \beta + \gamma = -\frac{b}{a}, \quad \alpha\beta + \beta\gamma + \gamma\alpha = \frac{c}{a}, \quad \alpha\beta\gamma = -\frac{d}{a}. \] Useful identity for sum of squares of roots: \(\alpha^2 + \beta^2 + \gamma^2 = (\alpha+\beta+\gamma)^2 - 2(\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha)\).

Modulus Inequalities Strategy:

  • \(|f(x)| \le g(x) \iff -g(x) \le f(x) \le g(x)\) (with condition \(g(x) \ge 0\)).
  • \(|f(x)| \ge g(x) \iff f(x) \le -g(x) \text{ or } f(x) \ge g(x)\).
  • \(|f(x)| < |g(x)| \iff [f(x)]^2 < [g(x)]^2 \iff [f(x) - g(x)][f(x) + g(x)] < 0\) (squaring both sides is valid because both sides are non-negative).

label.en: ▲ Level 3 University Rigor — Theorem: Rational Asymptotics & Complex Factorization

body.en:
Asymptotics of Rational Functions: Consider the rational function \(R(x) = \frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}\) where \(P, Q\) share no common factors:

  • Vertical Asymptotes: Occur at every real zero of \(Q(x)\). Near each root \(x = c\), \(\lim_{x\to c} |R(x)| = \infty\). If \(P(x)\) and \(Q(x)\) share a common factor \((x - c)^k\), cancellation leaves a removable singularity (hole) at \(x = c\) if the multiplicity in \(P\) is \(\ge\) multiplicity in \(Q\).
  • Horizontal Asymptotes: If \(\deg(P) < \deg(Q)\), the \(x\)-axis \(y = 0\) is the horizontal asymptote. If \(\deg(P) = \deg(Q)\), the horizontal asymptote is \(y = \frac{a_n}{b_n}\) (ratio of leading coefficients).
  • Oblique (Slant) Asymptotes: If \(\deg(P) = \deg(Q) + 1\), polynomial long division yields: \[ R(x) = mx + c + \frac{R_0(x)}{Q(x)}, \quad \text{where } \deg(R_0) < \deg(Q). \] Since \(\lim_{x\to\pm\infty} \frac{R_0(x)}{Q(x)} = 0\), the linear function \(y = mx + c\) is an oblique asymptote.
  • Asymptote Crossing: A rational curve can intersect its non-vertical asymptote! Points of intersection with \(y = mx + c\) are determined by solving the remainder equation: \[ R(x) - (mx + c) = 0 \iff R_0(x) = 0. \]
  • Range via Quadratic Discriminant: To find the range of \(y = \frac{ax^2+bx+c}{dx^2+ex+f}\), rearrange into a quadratic in \(x\): \((yd - a)x^2 + (ye - b)x + (yf - c) = 0\). For real \(x\) to exist, the discriminant must satisfy \(\Delta(y) = [ye - b]^2 - 4(yd - a)(yf - c) \ge 0\). The resulting polynomial inequality determines the exact range of \(y\).

label.en: ◆ Why It Works — First-Principles Derivation (Functions (HL Extensions))

body.en:
Why Completing the Square & Log-Linearization Work: Any quadratic \(f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c\) (\(a \ne 0\)) can be rewritten by factoring \(a\) from the first two terms and adding/subtracting \((b/2a)^2\):

\[ ax^2 + bx + c = a\!\left(x + \frac{b}{2a}\right)^2 + \left(c - \frac{b^2}{4a}\right) \]

Because \(\left(x + \frac{b}{2a}\right)^2 \ge 0\) for all \(x \in \mathbb{R}\), the extreme value \(k = c - \frac{b^2}{4a}\) is attained uniquely at the axis of symmetry \(x = -\frac{b}{2a}\), restricting the range to \([k, \infty)\) (if \(a > 0\)) and making \(f\) invertible on \(x \ge -\frac{b}{2a}\). Similarly, applying \(\ln\) to power laws \(y = ax^n\) yields \(\ln y = n\ln x + \ln a\), transforming a nonlinear curve into a straight line of gradient \(n\).

label.en: Worked Example 2.1 — Analytical Solution of Modulus Equation

solution.en:
1. Geometric sketch: \(y = |2x - 4|\) is a V-shaped curve with vertex at \((2, 0)\), \(y\)-intercept at \((0, 4)\), and rays \(y = 2x - 4\) for \(x \ge 2\) and \(y = -(2x - 4) = 4 - 2x\) for \(x < 2\).

2. Pre-condition: \(|2x - 4| \ge 0 \implies x + 1 \ge 0 \implies x \ge -1\).

3. Case 1 (\(x \ge 2\)):
\[ 2x - 4 = x + 1 \implies x = 5. \] Check: \(5 \ge 2\), and \(|2(5) - 4| = 6 = 5 + 1\). Valid! ✓

4. Case 2 (\(x < 2\)):
\[ -(2x - 4) = x + 1 \implies 4 - 2x = x + 1 \implies 3x = 3 \implies x = 1. \] Check: \(1 < 2\), and \(|2(1) - 4| = |-2| = 2 = 1 + 1\). Valid! ✓

Solutions: \(x = 1\) and \(x = 5\).

label.en: Worked Example 2.2 — Complex Factorization & Vieta Verification

problem.en: Given that \(p(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 + 7x - 5\) has a root \(x = 1\), find all roots and verify Vieta's formulas.

solution.en:
1. Since \(x = 1\) is a root, \((x - 1)\) is a factor. Perform synthetic or polynomial division: \[ x^3 - 3x^2 + 7x - 5 = (x - 1)(x^2 - 2x + 5). \] 2. Find the roots of the quadratic factor \(x^2 - 2x + 5 = 0\): \[ x = \frac{2 \pm \sqrt{(-2)^2 - 4(1)(5)}}{2} = \frac{2 \pm \sqrt{4 - 20}}{2} = \frac{2 \pm 4i}{2} = 1 \pm 2i. \] Thus the three roots are \(\alpha = 1\), \(\beta = 1 + 2i\), \(\gamma = 1 - 2i\).

3. Verify Vieta's Formulas:
Sum of roots: \(\alpha + \beta + \gamma = 1 + (1+2i) + (1-2i) = 3 = -\frac{-3}{1}\). ✓
Sum of pairwise products: \[ \alpha\beta + \beta\gamma + \gamma\alpha = 1(1+2i) + (1+2i)(1-2i) + 1(1-2i) = (1+2i) + (1+4) + (1-2i) = 7 = \frac{7}{1}. \quad \checkmark \] Product of roots: \[ \alpha\beta\gamma = 1(1+4) = 5 = -\frac{-5}{1}. \quad \checkmark \]

label.en: Worked Example 2.3 — Oblique Asymptote of Rational Function

problem.en: Find the oblique asymptote of \(f(x) = \dfrac{2x^2 + 3x - 1}{x - 1}\) and determine whether the curve intersects it.

solution.en:
1. Divide \(2x^2 + 3x - 1\) by \(x - 1\) using polynomial long division: \[ \begin{array}{r} 2x + 5 \quad \\ x - 1 {\overline{\smash{\big)}\,2x^2 + 3x - 1}} \\ \underline{-(2x^2 - 2x)} \phantom{-1} \\ 5x - 1 \\ \underline{-(5x - 5)} \\ 4 \end{array} \] 2. Express \(f(x)\) in quotient-remainder form: \[ f(x) = 2x + 5 + \frac{4}{x - 1}. \] 3. As \(x \to \pm\infty\), \(\frac{4}{x - 1} \to 0\). Therefore, the oblique asymptote is \(y = 2x + 5\).

4. Check for intersection: set \(f(x) = 2x + 5\): \[ 2x + 5 + \frac{4}{x - 1} = 2x + 5 \implies \frac{4}{x - 1} = 0. \] Since \(\frac{4}{x - 1} \neq 0\) for any real \(x\), the curve never intersects its oblique asymptote.

label.en: ⚠ Topic 2 Exam Traps: Modulus & Inverse Functions

body.en:
Squaring Modulus Equations: While squaring both sides of \(|ax+b| = |cx+d|\) is convenient, squaring when one side is variable without modulus (e.g. \(|2x-3| = x-1\)) can introduce extraneous roots. Always check candidates in the un-squared equation.

Self-Inverse Functions: For rational functions of the form \(f(x) = \dfrac{ax+b}{cx-a}\), \(f(x) = f^{-1}(x)\). Recognize this symmetry immediately to save algebraic time.

Domain Restrictions on Inverses: For quadratic functions, an inverse function only exists if the domain is restricted to one side of the vertex (e.g. \(x \ge h\)). Stating \(f^{-1}\) without stating its restricted domain \(x \ge k\) loses marks.

Worked Example (AA HL Paper 1 — 8 marks):
Consider $f(x) = \frac{x^2 - 3x + 6}{x - 1}$ for $x \ne 1$.
(a) Express $f(x)$ in the form $x + a + \frac{b}{x - 1}$ and hence state the equation of the oblique asymptote. [3]
(b) Find the coordinates of the local maximum and local minimum points on the graph of $f$, and hence state the range of $f$. [5]

Official IB Markscheme Solution:
(a) $x^2 - 3x + 6 = (x - 1)(x - 2) + 4 \implies f(x) = x - 2 + \frac{4}{x - 1}$ ($a = -2, b = 4$) [M1] [A1]
Oblique asymptote is $y = x - 2$ [A1]
(b) $f'(x) = 1 - \frac{4}{(x-1)^2} = 0 \implies (x-1)^2 = 4 \implies x - 1 = \pm 2 \implies x = 3$ or $x = -1$ [M1] [A1]
At $x = -1$, $f(-1) = -1 - 2 - 2 = -5$ (Local Max $(-1, -5)$); at $x = 3$, $f(3) = 3 - 2 + 2 = 3$ (Local Min $(3, 3)$) [A1] [A1]
Range of $f$: $(-\infty, -5] \cup [3, \infty)$ (or $y \le -5$ or $y \ge 3$) [A1]

rows.en: Confuses the product law \(\ln(xy) = \ln x + \ln y\) with a non-existent sum rule.
Only factor products, quotients, and powers inside logarithms: \(\ln(xy) = \ln x + \ln y\).
Keeping both roots of \(\sqrt{2x+6} = x - 2\) without checking \(x - 2 \ge 0\)
Squaring both sides loses the sign of \(x - {r}\), introducing roots where \(\sqrt{\cdot} = -\text{number}\).
Enforce the range condition \(x \ge 2\) before or after squaring.
Restricting domain of \(f(x) = (x-3)^2 + 1\) to \(x \ge 0\) for invertibility
The vertex is at \(x = 3\), so \(f(2) = f(4) = 2\) fails the horizontal line test on \(x \ge 0\).
Restrict the domain at the vertex axis of symmetry: \(x \ge 3\) (or \(x \le 3\)).

question.en: Find the exact range of \(f(x) = \dfrac{x}{x^2 + 1}\) for \(x \in \mathbb{R}\).

solution.en:
Let \(y = \frac{x}{x^2 + 1}\). Multiply both sides by \(x^2 + 1\) (valid since \(x^2 + 1 > 0\) for all \(x \in \mathbb{R}\)): \[ y(x^2 + 1) = x \implies yx^2 - x + y = 0. \] If \(y = 0\), \(-x = 0 \implies x = 0\), so \(0\) is in the range.
For \(y \neq 0\), this is a quadratic equation in \(x\). For real \(x\) to exist, the discriminant \(\Delta\) must be non-negative: \[ \Delta = (-1)^2 - 4(y)(y) = 1 - 4y^2 \ge 0. \] Solve the inequality: \[ 4y^2 \le 1 \implies y^2 \le \frac{1}{4} \implies -\frac{1}{2} \le y \le \frac{1}{2}. \] Thus the range of \(f(x)\) is \(\left[-\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right]\).

question.en: [Practice 2 · Medium] The diagram shows the graph of the function \( y = f(x) \). The equation of the function is given by \( f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c \). Given that the vertex of the parabola is at \( (-1, 8) \) and the graph passes through the point \( (1, 0) \), find the values of \( a \) and \( b \).

hints.en: Tier 1 (Conceptual Setup): Identify the governing relationship in Functions (HL Extensions) and start from \( y = f(x) \).
Tier 2 (Key Transformation): Apply the key algebraic/geometric step leading toward \( f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c \).
Tier 3 (Final Verification): Check signs, units, and domain restrictions on your result before opening the full solution below.

solution.en: The vertex of a parabola given by \( f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c \) is at \( \left( -\frac{b}{2a}, f\left(-\frac{b}{2a}\right) \right) \). We are given that the vertex is at \( (-1, 8) \). Therefore, \( -\frac{b}{2a} = -1 \), which implies \( b = 2a \). We are also given that the vertex is at \( y=8 \), so \( f(-1) = 8 \). Substituting \( x = -1 \) into the function: \( a(-1)^2 + b(-1) + c = 8 \implies a - b + c = 8 \). Since \( b = 2a \), we have \( a - 2a + c = 8 \implies -a + c = 8 \). The graph also passes through the point \( (1, 0) \). So, \( f(1) = 0 \). Substituting \( x = 1 \) into the function: \( a(1)^2 + b(1) + c = 0 \implies a + b + c = 0 \). Now we have a system of equations: 1) \( b = 2a \) 2) \( -a + c = 8 \) 3) \( a + b + c = 0 \) Substitute (1) into (3): \( a + 2a + c = 0 \implies 3a + c = 0 \). Now we have a system with \( a \) and \( c \): -a + c = 8 3a + c = 0 Subtract the first equation from the second: \( (3a + c) - (-a + c) = 0 - 8 \implies 4a = -8 \implies a = -2 \). Substitute \( a = -2 \) into \( b = 2a \): \( b = 2(-2) = -4 \). So, \( a = -2 \) and \( b = -4 \). Common algebraic traps include: - Incorrectly applying the vertex formula. - Errors in solving the system of linear equations. - Confusing the x and y coordinates of the vertex. [M1] [A1] Answer: a = -2, b = -4.

question.en: [Practice 3 · Medium] Find the oblique asymptote of \( f(x) = \dfrac{4x^{2} + 3x - 14}{(x + 2)} \), in the form \(y=mx+c\).

hints.en: Tier 1 (Conceptual Setup): Identify the governing relationship in Functions (HL Extensions) and start from \( f(x) = \dfrac{4x^{2} + 3x - 14}{(x + 2)} \).

solution.en: Working through this functions step: \( \text{Dividing: }\dfrac{4x^{2} + 3x - 14}{(x + 2)} = 4x - 5 + \dfrac{-4}{(x + 2)}\text{, so the asymptote is }y=4x - 5. \) [M1] [A1] Answer: \(y=4x - 5\).
